analysis.one_liner: Coal India is the world's largest coal miner, a government-controlled company that digs and sells thermal coal mostly to Indian power plants.
analysis.whats_happening: Q2 FY27 (Sept-2026 quarter) financial results have not been published as of 15-Oct-2026; only operational data is out, showing coal supply up 12% YoY to 186 MT and production up 3.8% YoY. The government completed a stake sale (OFS) in mid-2026 that trimmed its holding from ~63% to ~61%. A brokerage upgraded the stock in early October citing strong volumes and the pending Mahanadi Coalfields (MCL) listing, but the exact date of Q2 results has not been confirmed from available sources.
analysis.plain_terms: Coal India mines and sells coal, mainly to power companies, and the government owns about 61% of it. The stock pays a large dividend (6.35% yield) and looks statistically cheap at roughly 8x earnings, which is typical for a government-run commodity business facing long-term questions about coal's role in India's energy mix. The tension to watch: coal volumes are growing nicely, but costs (diesel, wages) are rising faster than revenue, so profit margins are getting squeezed even as the company sells more coal.
analysis.quarters: Q1 FY27 (June-2026 quarter) revenue rose 7.8% YoY to about ₹46,255 crore on 4% higher coal off-take, but EBITDA margin fell roughly 320 basis points to ~26% as diesel prices rose about 8.6% and a new non-executive wage revision (effective June-2026) began hitting costs - management flagged an estimated cumulative impact of around ₹3,400 crore through December 2026. PAT was roughly flat YoY. This is not comparable cleanly with FY26: full-year FY26 PAT fell 12.4% to ₹31,071 crore mainly because of a one-time executive pay-scale provision ordered by a court (retrospective to August 2023) and an impairment at a subsidiary (SECL) - this was an accounting/provisioning effect, not a drop in underlying coal demand, and should not be read as a business decline. One source cited this one-off provision at ₹1,458 crore and another at ₹2,201 crore - the exact figure could not be confirmed.
analysis.performance_read: Returns have been strong and are not distorted by any corporate action (no splits or demergers on record): the stock is up 16.9% over 1 year versus the Nifty's -10%, up 65% over 3 years versus Nifty's +14.6%, and up 244% over 5 years versus Nifty's +23%. It has also meaningfully beaten peer NMDC over 1, 3 and 5 years. Current price of ₹417 is 11.2% below its June-2026 peak of ₹469 but still within its 52-week range - this is a normal pullback, not a crash.
analysis.valuation_read: At roughly 8.3x trailing earnings and 2.2x book value, Coal India looks cheap next to the broader market. Why it's cheap: it is a government-controlled commodity producer where prices and volumes are partly policy-driven, earnings are cyclical, there is an ongoing government stake-sale overhang (the recent OFS cut the government's holding to ~61%, and more disinvestment is plausible), and coal carries a structural long-term question mark tied to the energy transition. Whether it is actually cheap depends on whether the ~6.35% dividend yield and high ROE/ROCE are sustainable once wage and cost pressures fully show up - that is not yet resolved.
analysis.growth_read: Growth so far is volume-led: coal supply was up 12% YoY and production up 3.8% YoY in the first half of FY27, with the company also drawing down about 63 million tonnes of pithead stock. But this volume growth is coinciding with margin compression (EBITDA margin down ~320 basis points in Q1 FY27) due to rising diesel costs and the new wage settlement, so revenue and tonnage are growing while profitability per tonne is under pressure - a less durable combination than growth where both volume and margin rise together.
analysis.health_read: Balance sheet health is strong: total borrowings of about ₹14,072 crore against reserves of about ₹1,12,939 crore confirm the company is close to debt-free, and ROE (28.2%) and ROCE (35%) are high. For Coal India, the risk that matters is business risk, not financial risk - specifically cost inflation (diesel, wages) and government-influenced pricing, not debt or cash conversion.
analysis.ownership_read: The Government of India remains the controlling shareholder at roughly 61% after trimming its stake via an OFS in mid-2026 (floor price ₹412, raising about ₹5,000 crore) from around 63%. As a PSU, there is no promoter pledging, consistent with expectations. FII holding is roughly 9.6-10.4% and DII holding roughly 22-23%, though exact current-quarter figures vary slightly across sources. No notable individually named large investor was found in the shareholding data reviewed.
strengths: Near debt-free balance sheet: borrowings of ~₹14,072 crore versus reserves of ~₹1.13 lakh crore
High capital efficiency: ROE ~28.2% and ROCE ~35%
Volume momentum: coal supply up 12% YoY and production up 3.8% YoY in H1 FY27
Outperformed the Nifty and peer NMDC by a wide margin over 1, 3 and 5 years (e.g., +244% vs Nifty's +23% over 5 years)
watchpoints: EBITDA margin compressed by roughly 320 basis points in Q1 FY27 on rising diesel costs and a new wage revision estimated to cost ~₹3,400 crore cumulatively through December 2026
FY26 PAT fell 12.4% to ₹31,071 crore, driven by a one-off court-ordered pay provision and an SECL impairment - not comparable cleanly to FY27 figures
Government stake reduced from ~63% to ~61% via a 2026 OFS, signalling a continuing supply overhang from potential further disinvestment
Coal India's earnings remain tied to government coal-pricing policy and the pace of India's energy transition, a structural risk beyond the company's control
analysis.one_thing: The Q2 FY27 (September-2026 quarter) financial results - date not yet confirmed - which will show whether the margin pressure from wage costs and diesel prices seen in Q1 FY27 continued despite the 12% YoY volume growth already reported operationally.
analysis.data_notes: Cross-checked: valuation ratios, debt levels and ROE/ROCE against Screener.in; return and price data taken as given and not recomputed. Could not verify: exact Q2 FY27 results date (not yet published as of 15-Oct-2026); the precise amount of the FY26 one-off wage provision (sources show ₹1,458 crore vs ₹2,201 crore); Q1 FY27 PAT varies slightly across sources (₹8,850-8,852 crore vs one outlier at ₹8,609 crore, with the Screener-derived figure treated as most reliable); EV/EBITDA multiple; AGM date; any strike activity in the last 3 months (no confirming or disconfirming source found). No company investor-presentation PDF was directly accessed in this round of research.
